item.title: Dead Man's Switch — a letter that opens only if you stop checking in (testnet) (1 posts)
item.description: Email drafts and paper envelopes both have the same flaw — somebody has to find them, and somebody can read them early. Dead Man’s Switch is a letter that opens only if you stop checking in. You write it, you name who receives it, and you pick how often you’ll confirm you’re still here. Every check-in pushes the deadline back. Miss it, and the letter goes out. Change your mind, and you cancel — and from that moment nobody can ever read it, including me. Try it on testnet: https://dead-man-switch.chainsolution.net (EN / FR / DE) How it works The letter is encrypted in your browser. It is never stored on chain and I never see it. What’s on chain is a cell you own, holding a deadline....

item.title: Ward: lock proof for CKB (1 posts)
item.description: An update to the last reply, where I said the verifier is Node only: since ckb-ward 0.5.0 it also runs in the browser. Hanssen pointed us to ckb-vm-js, which compiles CKB’s own transaction verifier and CKB-VM to WebAssembly. Ward now takes it as a lock runner, ckbVmJs(), through a new ckb-ward/browser entry. A site can check a proof inside the visitor’s page, reading only a public RPC, with no server of its own. Measured on 2026-11-16: every saved proof (16 locks, 3 of them on mainnet) gives the same result as the node’s own script VM, and the same cycles when accepted. In Chromium the lock runs in 16 to 57 ms; a whole check, with the chain reads, takes 1 to 2 s. ckb-vm-js is early and...

item.title: CLASP UPDATE (1 posts)
item.description: Hey everyone, I’m Drey, creator of Clasp, the permission layer for Fiber wallets that took first place in the Wallet & Payment UX Infrastructure category at Gone in 60ms and was named overall winner. A couple of days ago I did an AMA on r/NervosNetwork and talked about what comes next. Rather than come back here with a plan, we built the first part of it. This post covers what people asked, what’s now live, and what’s still missing. The problem, briefly If an app wants to make Fiber payments for you today, it needs access to your node’s RPC. item.title: Fiber LSP: Running Channels on the Server, Signing in the Wallet (2 posts)
item.description: We have tried to port a full Fiber node to different types of clients, and even connect it to CKB Light Client. In practice, however, clients have difficulty staying online all the time: an application may exit unexpectedly, the system may stop or suspend background processes, or the network may disconnect suddenly. Brief disconnections are especially common when a phone switches between Wi-Fi and mobile networks. Fiber uses payment channels to send and receive payments. Once a local node loses its network connection, it can no longer exchange messages with other nodes. New payments cannot be sent or received normally, and pending payments may time out and fail.
